A partner told me to stay out of their department.

And I listened.

On paper it made sense. Respect the lanes.

Let people lead their own areas.

But it wasn't about protecting their work.

It was about protecting their comfort.

I respected it. 

Because I didn't want the conflict.

Because I told myself they knew that space better than I did.

Because backing off felt like trust.

It wasn't.

When a partner asks you to stay out, and you have a reason to be in, that is not a healthy boundary. 

That is a warning sign.

The moment you stop asking questions in your own company is the moment someone else starts running it.

I didn't fight for it then.

I paid for that later.

I thought that was how you manage people well.

Know their craft. Understand their process. Speak their language.

What it actually did was make me a mediocre version of everyone on my team, and a worse version of myself.

Here is what I know now.

You don't need to know what they know.

You need to know enough to know they are doing it.

There is a difference between understanding enough to evaluate and knowing enough to compete.

One builds trust.

The other builds resentment.

Your job is to hire people who are genuinely better than you at their craft, then create the conditions for them to do it well.

You are not the expert. You are the standard-setter.

That shift took me years to get right.

But the moment it clicked, everything changed.

But somewhere along the way, I became the only one who actually cared what happened next.

Not in a dramatic way.

In a slow, quiet way that you don't notice until you're exhausted.

My partners were doing their jobs.

Executing well within their lanes.

Keeping clients happy, keeping the team fed.

But the vision, the next client, the next capability, the next version of what Tristeps could be?

That was only in my head.

And nothing moved.

That was the day I realised it wasn't a team problem.

It was a leadership problem.

Mine.

Not because the work got harder.

Because "good enough" got cheaper.

A client used to need a full team to produce a campaign.

Script. Shoot. Edit. Motion. Copy.

Now they can get 70% of that in an afternoon, with one prompt and a free tool.

The question is not whether AI is replacing creatives.

The question is: what are you still being paid for?

If your value is output, you're already competing with a machine.

The agencies surviving this aren't producing more.

They're producing work that actually means something. Work that requires judgment, context, and taste.

AI is fast. But it has no skin in the game.

Your client does.

I technically stopped selling only production time two years ago; it's a byproduct.

We started selling perspective.

That shift didn't happen overnight. 

But it's the reason we're still here.

At 32, I was the only one left standing.

Not because the business failed. Because I slowly realised I was the only one actually building it.

The team was there. The revenue was coming in. But somewhere along the way, everyone got comfortable.

Comfortable farming the same clients.

Comfortable staying in their lane. Comfortable letting me carry the vision alone.

And I let it happen. Because I didn't know how to lead it differently.

For years I thought the answer was better people. Better hires. Better partners.

What I didn't see was this: I was the bottleneck. Not them.

The moment I stopped trying to fix the people around me and started fixing how I led, everything changed.

I scaled my full-time team down to 1-2 folks. Revenue doubled.

Not because I worked harder. Because I finally got out of my own way.

I'm Henry. Director and Executive Producer at Tristeps Studios. 10 years in. Google APAC, Sony SEA, McDonald's Singapore, 3M Asia.
